source.title: Asymmetric Scaling Laws from Sparse Features

record.tranche_reason: The paper derives and measures a double-descent curve in a sparse random-feature model, a different model class and setting from the original deep-network studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a double-descent peak in its joint model-size/data-size scaling curve (Figure 2). It does not sweep training epochs. The discussion of label noise, regularization, and epoch-dependent effects is prospective or cites prior work, not a new test. Other reported scaling-exponent fits, including the nonlinear-feature experiments, establish asymmetry but do not themselves report a full double-descent curve. Cited results from other studies are not included.
record.test_reason: In a new setting (sparse-activation inputs, ridgeless min-norm sketched linear regression with frozen random features), the paper measures population loss across N and D. It reports a double-descent peak near the interpolation threshold N ≈ K(D) in the collapsed loss curve (Fig. 2) and in fixed-N data sweeps (Fig. 3). The double descent is a side result of a scaling-law study, not its target.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly wrong. The authors' main conclusion is that sparse input activations break scaling symmetry: they yield distinct exponents αN = α1+α2+1 and αD = αN/(α1+1), a data-favoring compute-optimal frontier, and a rare-spike GD failure law, and the asymmetry persists under ReLU features. The double-descent peak is presented as a feature of ridgeless interpolation, not of sparsity (footnote 8). Sparsity only sets its location, at N ≈ K(D).
record.recipe_differences: The paper analyzes sparse random-feature regression and a nonlinear random-feature experiment, rather than reproducing the original deep-network experiments or their method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported peak location depends on the sparsity exponent α1 through ξcrit; this paper does not report an epoch-dependent sensitivity analysis.
record.problems: The peak evidence in Figure 2 is presented graphically without tabulated loss values or an uncertainty estimate. The tested setting is a sparse random-feature model, not a broad survey of deep networks or model classes.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results bearing directly on the listed claim versions were extracted. The paper's separate exponent fits and nonlinear-feature asymmetry results do not report a full double-descent curve; discussion of epochs, noise, and regularization is not a new test.

untested.parts: No deep or trained-feature networks; only linear and frozen-ReLU random features. The ReLU experiments report exponents, not a peak.
No test-error sweep over training epochs.
Only the ridgeless sparse random-feature model at (α1, α2) = (1.0, 0.3).
Only one model class: linear random features with sparse power-law inputs.
Epoch axis, and any model-side effective-complexity measure. The threshold uses a data-side count K(D) of observed coordinates.
Label noise, tuned ridge regularization, and multiple peaks are not tested. Smoothing by regularization or early stopping is only cited (footnote 8, Hastie et al.).

missing.what: Fixed-N test-loss-vs-compute curves (D swept) each show a double-descent spike before approaching the frontier. This is direct evidence that more data hurts near threshold.

record.verdict_notes: The peak arises with a noiseless teacher. The variance comes from unobserved coordinates, consistent with V6's variance reading, but V6 is not tested. The record's tranche T2 is changed to T3, because this is a new setting rather than a different method on the original question. No numbers are tabulated for the peak height.

versions.untested_parts: The paper studies random features and a two-layer network with frozen random first-layer weights, but does not report a model-size double-descent result specifically for deep networks.
No test-error sweep over training epochs is reported.
The peak is reported in a joint scaling curve; the paper does not provide a separately tabulated fixed-model-size data sweep through the peak.
Tests the general double-descent shape in the paper's sparse random-feature setting, not across a broad range of model classes.

Relates the size/data interpolation threshold to the effective count of learnable coordinates K(D); does not test epoch-wise peak location or whether one measure predicts peak location along every axis.
Label noise, tuned regularization, and multiple or split peaks are not tested in the paper's experiments.
The paper does not re-express complexity using an alternative effective parameter count to test whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: sparse random-feature model
rows.size_stated: N and D varied across a wide range; specific values not stated for Figure 2
rows.operation_detail: Measured population loss across model size N and dataset size D, and plotted the rescaled loss against the dimensionless ratio ξ.

conditions.value: ridgeless population loss of the sparse random-feature model

rows.measure: Rescaled population loss curve; the text reports a sharp double-descent peak near the interpolation threshold, where N matches the number of activated, learnable coordinates K(D).
rows.value: Peak location: ξcrit = 1/Γ(α1/(1+α1)); the plotted loss values are figure only.
rows.note: The text explicitly describes a prominent peak and identifies its location. The joint curve supports the more-data-can-hurt result near the threshold and the general double-descent result in this random-feature model. The effective-coordinate account uses K(D), with N matching K(D) at the threshold.
rows.check: Subject is a linear random-feature (sketched least-squares) model with noiseless targets, not a network. The peak is shown only graphically, with no loss values or baseline. The data-axis reading (V3) is inferred from the collapsed curve: at fixed N, raising D moves ξ through ξcrit. The direct fixed-N D-sweep evidence is in Fig. 3 and is not captured by this row.
